standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.2.5, the sentence 'If any subset of the models ... jointly characterize the conditional distribution of $Y$, then this estimator is consistent and asymptotically efficient', as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 199 (PDF p. 217), second paragraph; the mixture and its parameter vector: pp. 198–199 (PDF pp. 216–217)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] ... where $\boldsymbol\theta = (p_1, \boldsymbol\theta_1, p_2, \boldsymbol\theta_2, ..., p_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_{M-1}, \boldsymbol\theta_M)$. Then, as before, $\prod_{i=1}^{n} g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \boldsymbol\theta)$ can be maximized to find the ML estimate of $\boldsymbol\theta$. (This can sometimes be computationally tricky.) If any subset of the models in $(g_1(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_1), ..., g_M(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_M))$ jointly characterize the conditional distribution of $Y$, then this estimator is consistent and asymptotically efficient. [What is refuted] That correct specification by a proper subset of the components implies consistency (and regular efficiency) of the ML estimator of the displayed full parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$. The claim under the identification and uniqueness conditions of Theorem 5.2.6 is not refuted. [Counterexample, from the validators] Let $Y$ take values in $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ with no covariates, and let $g_1(y; a) = 1 - a$ for $y = 0$, $a$ for $y = 1$, $0$ for $y \in \{2, 3\}$; $g_2(y; b) = 0$ for $y \in \{0, 1\}$, $1 - b$ for $y = 2$, $b$ for $y = 3$; $g(y; \boldsymbol\theta) = pg_1(y; a) + (1 - p)g_2(y; b)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta = (p, a, b) \in \boldsymbol\Theta = [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [\frac{1}{4}, \frac{3}{4}]$ (compact; the likelihood is continuous and bounded by 1; a maximum exists). The four masses are $(p(1 - a), pa, (1 - p)(1 - b), (1 - p)b)$. Take $\boldsymbol\theta_A = (1, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{4})$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_B = (1, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{3}{4})$. Then: (a) both give the PMF $(\frac{2}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, 0, 0)$, so the first component alone characterizes the distribution of $Y$ and the printed hypothesis holds at both; (b) for every $n$ and every sample, the joint probability of the sample is the same under $\boldsymbol\theta_A$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_B$ (equal to $(\frac{1}{3})^k(\frac{2}{3})^{n-k}$ for a sample of zeros and ones with $k$ ones); (c) for any estimator $T_n = (\hat p_n, \hat a_n, \hat b_n)$, the events $\{|\hat b_n - \frac{1}{4}| < \frac{1}{8}\}$ and $\{|\hat b_n - \frac{3}{4}| < \frac{1}{8}\}$ are disjoint and have the same probabilities under the two parameter vectors, so $\Pr_{\boldsymbol\theta_A}[|\hat b_n - \frac{1}{4}| < \frac{1}{8}] + \Pr_{\boldsymbol\theta_B}[|\hat b_n - \frac{3}{4}| < \frac{1}{8}] \le 1$ for every $n$; hence no estimator, and in particular no ML selection, is consistent for $\boldsymbol\theta$ at both $\boldsymbol\theta_A$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_B$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] Parametric Model. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: All steps are exact for each $n$: the four masses sum to 1; at $p = 1$ they do not depend on $b$; the two probability measures on samples coincide; and $\frac{1}{2} = |\frac{3}{4} - \frac{1}{4}| < \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8}$ is false, so the two events are disjoint. For $0 < p < 1$ the vector is recovered from the masses $q_j$ by $p = q_0 + q_1$, $a = q_1/p$, $b = q_3/(1 - p)$, so the failure is confined to the zero-weight boundary.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate. History of the validation: two validators confirmed; an adjudication read the sentence as inheriting the identification and uniqueness conditions of Theorem 5.2.6 and recorded 'not confirmed'; the highest-effort check (runs/P001/validate/P001-C05-N005/doubt/doubt.json) restored the confirmation for the operative reading, in which 'this estimator' is the ML estimate of the displayed full vector: in exactly the case the sentence names, unused components can take zero weight and their free parameters are not identified. The adjudicator's point stands that no counterexample satisfies the inherited uniqueness premise. The doubt artifact also gives a positive-support rational example with identical four-outcome laws at two parameter vectors.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 5.2.5, the 'any subset' sentence, corrected: consistency and efficiency of the mixture ML estimator under identification of the full parameter vector
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected sentence] Correct specification by a subset alone does not guarantee consistency or efficiency of the displayed full parameter vector. If the fitted mixture is correctly specified, its true full parameter is identifiable and interior in independent coordinates, and the conditions for ML consistency and regular information-bound efficiency hold (including nonsingular information), its ML estimator is consistent and asymptotically efficient. Freely parameterized unused components must be excluded or removed before the full-vector claim is applied. [Formal content] Let $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} p_mg_m(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta_m)$ with $p_M = 1 - \sum_{m<M} p_m$. (i) Non-identification: if distinct $\boldsymbol\theta$ and $\boldsymbol\theta'$ lie in the parameter space, have the same weights with $p_j = 0$, and differ only in $\boldsymbol\theta_j$, then $g(\cdot, \cdot; \boldsymbol\theta) = g(\cdot, \cdot; \boldsymbol\theta')$, the distribution of every sample is the same under both for every $n$, $\mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta)] = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta')]$, and no estimator converges in probability to $\boldsymbol\theta$ under $\boldsymbol\theta$ and to $\boldsymbol\theta'$ under $\boldsymbol\theta'$. (ii) Consistency under identification: if the model is true at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, the fitted parameter space is compact, $L(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$ is continuous and uniquely maximized at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, and $\sup_{\mathbf{t}}|L_n(\mathbf{t}) - L(\mathbf{t})| \xrightarrow{p} 0$, then every measurable maximizer $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ of $L_n$ satisfies $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta^0$. (iii) Normality and efficiency under explicit regularity: assume the conditions in (ii), take a measurable ML maximizer, and suppose that $\boldsymbol\theta^0$ is interior in independent coordinates. Let $P_0$ be the true observation law. Assume that there is one measurable set $S$ with $P_0(S)=1$ on which $g(y,\mathbf x;\mathbf t)>0$ for every $\mathbf t$ in the fitted parameter space, that the log likelihoods are integrable under $P_0$, and that, for every $(\mathbf x,y)\in S$, $\mathbf t\mapsto\log g(y,\mathbf x;\mathbf t)$ is $C^2$ on a common open neighborhood of $\boldsymbol\theta^0$. Differentiation under the integral is valid, the score $s=\nabla\log g(Y,\mathbf X;\boldsymbol\theta^0)$ has finite second moment and $\mathrm E_0[s]=0$, and $I=\mathrm E_0[ss^T]$ is positive definite. Assume also that every entry of the log-likelihood Hessian is integrable throughout that neighborhood, that its population expectation $H(\mathbf t)=\mathrm E_0[\nabla^2\log g(Y,\mathbf X;\mathbf t)]$ is continuous at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, that $H(\boldsymbol\theta^0)=-I$, and that the average sample Hessians converge uniformly in probability to $H$ on that neighborhood. Then $\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}-\boldsymbol\theta^0)\xrightarrow{d}N(0,I^{-1})$. For the information-bound conclusion, additionally assume that the normalized conditional model, with a fixed covariate law and a fixed dominating measure, is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$ with score $s$. Then $I^{-1}$ is a lower bound, in the positive-semidefinite order, for the asymptotic covariance of every regular asymptotically linear estimator with a mean-zero, square-integrable influence function.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] Parametric Model. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood. [Theorem 5.2.6, p. 193 (PDF p. 211)] If the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ is true and some requisite regularity conditions (such as having a continuous likelihood function, a compact parameter space, and a unique maximum) are satisfied, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta$. [p. 194] $L_n(\mathbf{t}) = \frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ and $L(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$. $P_0$ is the joint law of $Z=(\mathbf X,Y)$ at $\boldsymbol\theta^0$, and all expectations in (iii) are under this law. The conditional densities are measurable, nonnegative and normalized in $y$ with respect to a fixed measure $\kappa$; the covariate law $\nu_X$ does not depend on the parameter. Write $p_{\mathbf t}(\mathbf x,y)=g(y,\mathbf x;\mathbf t)$ and $\lambda=\nu_X\otimes\kappa$. Differentiability in quadratic mean with score $s$ means $\int[\sqrt{p_{\boldsymbol\theta^0+u}}-\sqrt{p_{\boldsymbol\theta^0}}-\tfrac12u^Ts\sqrt{p_{\boldsymbol\theta^0}}]^2\,d\lambda=o(\|u\|^2)$. A regular asymptotically linear estimator $T_n$ here is measurable and has a measurable influence function $\psi$ with $\mathrm E_0[\psi]=0$, $\mathrm E_0[\|\psi\|^2]<\infty$ and $\sqrt n(T_n-\boldsymbol\theta^0)-n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\psi(Z_i)\xrightarrow{p}0$ under $P_0$; for every fixed vector $a$, under the model at $\boldsymbol\theta^0+a/\sqrt n$, $\sqrt n\{T_n-(\boldsymbol\theta^0+a/\sqrt n)\}$ has the same limiting law $N(0,\operatorname{Cov}_0(\psi))$. Thus the bound in (iii) is $\operatorname{Cov}_0(\psi)-I^{-1}\succeq0$. The common set $S$ and the identities $\mathrm E_0[s]=0$ and $H(\boldsymbol\theta^0)=-I$ are explicit assumptions, not consequences asserted from pointwise twice differentiability alone. In the QMD integral, $s\sqrt{p_{\boldsymbol\theta^0}}$ is set to zero where $p_{\boldsymbol\theta^0}=0$; the score can be assigned any value on this null-support set.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 15 (hot deck imputation: 'the bootstrap standard errors are likely to adequately characterize sampling variability', with the bootstrap's failure attributed to slowly converging bias), as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 233 (PDF p. 251), footnote 15, attached to the hot deck estimate; Table 6.3.1, row 'Hot Deck Imputation'. Hot deck imputation: Section 6.2.3, pp. 224–225 (PDF pp. 242–243). The bootstrap: Section 3.4.3, p. 131 (PDF p. 149)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [Footnote 15] The bootstrap may not work as a method for computing valid confidence intervals for hot deck imputation since the bias of the estimator may converge slowly (see, e.g., Abadie and Imbens 2008), but the bootstrap standard errors are likely to adequately characterize sampling variability. [Table 6.3.1] Hot Deck Imputation: Estimate 8.538, Bootstrap SE 1.204. [What is refuted] The general assurance, read as: for nearest-neighbour hot deck imputation the difficulty with the bootstrap is confined to bias, and the bootstrap standard error is a consistent estimate of the standard error when bias is not a problem. The reported numbers 8.538 and 1.204 are not shown to be wrong. [Counterexample, from the validator] For every $n$, draw i.i.d. units as follows: $P$ is uniform on $[\frac{1}{4}, \frac{3}{4}]$; conditional on $P = p$, $R$ is Bernoulli($p$); independently of $(P, R)$, $\varepsilon$ is $+1$ or $-1$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each; $Y = 50 + \varepsilon$. Take the covariate $X = P$, so the propensity score is $p_R(X) = P$; MAR, overlap and MCAR all hold, and $\mathrm{E}[Y] = 50$. Hot deck estimator $T_n$: for each unit with $R = 0$ impute the outcome of the unit with $R = 1$ nearest in $|P|$-distance (with replacement), and take the mean of the $n$ completed outcomes ($T_n = 50$ if no unit responded). Bootstrap: draw $n$ units with replacement, recompute the matches with the known scores, and let $\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)$ be the variance of the bootstrap estimate conditional on the sample. Then: (a) $\mathrm{E}[T_n] = 50$ exactly, for every $n$ (zero bias); (b) $\lim_{n \to \infty} n\mathrm{Var}(T_n) = V = 3\log 3 - \frac{1}{4} \approx 3.0458$, so $\sqrt{n}(T_n - 50) = O_p(1)$; (c) $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathrm{E}[n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)] = V_b = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{A}{2} + B\left(2\log 3 - \frac{3}{2}\right) \approx 2.6471$, where $s = 1 - e^{-1}$, $A = \frac{2}{s} - \frac{s}{2 - s}$ and $B = \frac{3}{2s} - \frac{4 - s}{2(2 - s)}$; (d) $A < 3$ and $B < \frac{3}{2}$, hence $V_b < V$; (e) $\sup_n\mathrm{E}[(n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*))^2] < \infty$, so $n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)$ is uniformly integrable and cannot converge in probability to $V$. The ordinary bootstrap variance, and hence the bootstrap standard error, is inconsistent for an exactly unbiased, root-$n$ consistent hot deck estimator.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the stable outcomes model $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ with response indicator $R_i$ (Definition 6.1.1); i.i.d. sampling of units; MCAR (Definition 6.1.5); MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 6.1.8) and conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); the response propensity function $p_R$ (Definition 6.1.11); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] Stable Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] Response Propensity Function. Suppose we observe $(R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Then the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. The random variable $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ is known as the propensity score for unit $i$. [Section 6.2.3, pp. 224–225] Hot deck imputation, using nearest-neighbor matching with the propensity score (which, for the moment, we assume is known): for each missing unit, find the observed unit that is closest on $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ and use that unit's outcome to fill in the missing outcome; the hot deck imputation estimate of $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ is the sample mean with the missing values imputed. [Section 3.4.3, p. 131] the bootstrap: take a with replacement sample of size $n$ from the sample, calculate the estimate using this bootstrap sample, repeat, and calculate the standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution of the estimator. [Definition 3.2.32, pp. 113–114 (PDF pp. 131–132)] consistency of a sampling variance estimator at the scale $n$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Exact, for each $n$; validator's derivation, Section 3] Let $K_j$ be the number of nonrespondents matched to respondent $j$, $W_j = 1 + K_j$ if $R_j = 1$ and $W_j = 0$ otherwise. Then $T_n - 50 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j W_j\varepsilon_j$; the weights depend only on $(P, R)$, so $\mathrm{E}[T_n|P, R] = 50$ and $n\mathrm{Var}(T_n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j\mathrm{E}[W_j^2]$. With bootstrap weights $W_j^*$: $T_n^* - 50 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j W_j^*\varepsilon_j$ and $\mathrm{E}[n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j\left\{\mathrm{E}[(W_j^*)^2] - \mathrm{E}[W_j^{(1)}W_j^{(2)}]\right\}$ for two conditionally independent bootstrap draws. [Limit constants] with $r = (1 - p)/p$: $\mathrm{E}[(1 + K)^2] \to 1 + 3r + \frac{3}{2}r^2$, giving $V = \int_{1/4}^{3/4} 2p[1 + 3r + \frac{3}{2}r^2]dp = 3\log 3 - \frac{1}{4}$; $U - H = 1 + Ar + Br^2$, giving $V_b = \mathrm{E}[P + A(1 - P) + B(1 - P)^2/P]$. With $q = e^{-1}$: $A - 3 = \frac{2(q^2 + 2q - 1)}{1 - q^2}$ and $B - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{4q^2 + 5q - 3}{2(1 - q^2)}$, both negative because $0 < q < \frac{3}{8}$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate (kind: statistical; an interpretive assurance resting on an exact counterexample). The limits in (b) and (c) come from a local Poisson-process analysis in the validator's derivation (Sections 4–8), checked symbolically by its script; they are asymptotic statements whose proofs are long, and are not re-derived here. The example uses known propensity scores, as Section 6.2.3 does; it does not reproduce the fitted-score procedure behind the entry 1.204, whose calibration remains unestablished. An external check of the cited paper is recorded in runs/P001/settle/settled.json.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Footnote 15, corrected: for hot deck (nearest-neighbour) imputation the ordinary bootstrap can give inconsistent standard errors even without bias
canonical_claim.location: p. 233 (PDF p. 251), footnote 15; Table 6.3.1, row 'Hot Deck Imputation'
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected footnote] The bootstrap may not work as a method for computing valid confidence intervals for hot deck imputation. With fixed-neighbor matching the ordinary bootstrap can give invalid variance estimates even when the estimator has no bias (see, e.g., Abadie and Imbens 2008); the bootstrap standard error reported here has no demonstrated calibration. [Formal content of the corrected claim] (i) Zero bias and root-$n$ consistency of a hot deck estimator do not imply that the bootstrap variance is consistent: there is an i.i.d. design satisfying MAR (indeed MCAR) and overlap, with a scalar continuously distributed known propensity score and bounded outcomes, for which the nearest-neighbour hot deck estimator $T_n$ satisfies $\mathrm{E}[T_n] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i]$ for every $n$ and $n\mathrm{Var}(T_n) \to V \in (0, \infty)$, while the conditional bootstrap variance satisfies $\mathrm{E}[n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)] \to V_b$ with $V_b < V$ and $n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)$ does not converge in probability to $V$ (the counterexample target for this finding, with $V = 3\log 3 - \frac{1}{4}$ and $V_b \approx 2.6471$). (ii) In that design, for every $n$, conditionally on the scores and responses the estimator is a weighted sum of independent mean-zero outcome deviations, $T_n - \mathrm{E}[Y_i] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j W_j\varepsilon_j$, with $W_j = 1 +$ (number of nonrespondents matched to respondent $j$), so $\mathrm{Var}(T_n|P, R) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{j : R_j = 1} W_j^2$ (the outcome deviations having variance 1).

[Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] Stable Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] Response Propensity Function. Suppose we observe $(R_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Then the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. The random variable $p_R(\mathbf{X}_i)$ is known as the propensity score for unit $i$. [Section 6.2.3, pp. 224–225 (PDF pp. 242–243)] hot deck imputation by nearest-neighbor matching on the propensity score. [Section 3.4.3, p. 131 (PDF p. 149)] the bootstrap standard deviation. [Definition 3.2.32, pp. 113–114] consistency of sampling variance and standard error estimators.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: As in the counterexample target: $T_n - 50 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j W_j\varepsilon_j$, $n\mathrm{Var}(T_n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j\mathrm{E}[W_j^2]$, and $\mathrm{E}[n\mathrm{Var}_*(T_n^*)] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_j\{\mathrm{E}[(W_j^*)^2] - \mathrm{E}[W_j^{(1)}W_j^{(2)}]\}$, exact for each $n$.
canonical_claim.note: Error rated Moderate. The correction withdraws an assurance; it does not supply a replacement standard error, and does not show the entry 1.204 to be wrong. The formal content is therefore a negative (existence) statement plus the exact conditional-variance identity that explains it: a donor's weight depends on how many recipients it serves, and resampling changes that count in a way the bootstrap does not reproduce. The parallel finding for matching in Chapter 7 is P001-C07-E011.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.2.4 (matching with estimated propensity scores: the bootstrap's failure attributed to slowly shrinking bias) and footnote 20 ('the bootstrap standard errors are likely to adequately characterize sampling variability'), as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 264 (PDF p. 282), end of Section 7.2.4, with footnote 13; p. 279 (PDF p. 297), footnote 20; p. 280 (PDF p. 298), Table 7.5.1, row 'Matching'. Matching: Section 7.2.4, pp. 262–263 (PDF pp. 280–281)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statements] [p. 264] However, matching estimators are not plug-in estimators, and so their properties do not operate quite as expected. For example, even if we have a consistent estimator of $p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$, matching with estimated propensity scores is not generally root-$n$ consistent—the bias (and therefore MSE) of the estimator shrinks “too slowly” as $n$ grows large—and, thus, the usual methods for constructing confidence intervals, including the bootstrap, do not generally work.$^{13}$ [Footnote 13] See, e.g., Abadie and Imbens (2008). [p. 279, footnote 20] As with hot deck imputation, the bootstrap may not work as a method for computing valid confidence intervals for matching estimators since the bias of the estimator may converge very slowly (see, e.g., Abadie and Imbens 2008), but the bootstrap standard errors are likely to adequately characterize sampling variability. [Table 7.5.1, Matching] $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)]$: Estimate 34.732, SE 1.951; $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$: Estimate 2.009, SE 1.988. [What is refuted] The assurance, read as: for one-to-one nearest-neighbour propensity score matching the bootstrap's difficulty is a matter of bias, and its standard error is a consistent estimate of the standard error when bias is not a problem. The statement that consistency of the score estimate alone does not ensure a root-$n$ rate is not refuted, and the reported numbers are not shown to be wrong. [Counterexample, from the validator] Draw i.i.d. units with $X \sim \mathrm{Uniform}[0, \frac{1}{2}]$, $D|X = x \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\frac{1}{4} + x)$, and $\varepsilon \in \{-1, +1\}$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each, independent of $(X, D)$; $Y(0) = \varepsilon$, $Y(1) = 0$, $Y = (1 - D)\varepsilon$; $\theta = \mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)] = 0$. Strong ignorability holds, the propensity score $p_D(X) = \frac{1}{4} + X$ is uniform on $[\frac{1}{4}, \frac{3}{4}]$, and outcomes are bounded. Estimated score: $\hat p_n(x) = \hat a_n + x$ with $\hat a_n = \mathrm{clip}_{[1/8, 3/8]}(\overline{D} - \overline{X})$, so $\hat a_n \xrightarrow{p} \frac{1}{4}$ and $|\hat p_n(x) - \hat p_n(z)| = |x - z|$: the estimated score gives exactly the same nearest-neighbour matches as the true score, in the sample and in every bootstrap resample. Matching estimator $\hat\theta_n$ (Section 7.2.4): impute $Y(0)$ of each treated unit by the outcome of the nearest control, and $Y(1)$ of each control by the outcome of the nearest treated unit (zero here); then $\hat\theta_n = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i : D_i = 0} W_i\varepsilon_i$ with $W_i = 1 + K_i$, $K_i$ the number of treated units matched to control $i$. Then: (a) $\mathrm{E}[\hat\theta_n] = 0 = \theta$ for every $n$ (zero bias); (b) $\lim_{n \to \infty} n\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta_n) = V = 3\log 3 - \frac{1}{4} \approx 3.0458$, so $\hat\theta_n$ is root-$n$ consistent; (c) the conditional bootstrap variance $V_n^*$ satisfies $\lim_{n \to \infty}\mathrm{E}[nV_n^*] = V_B = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{c_1}{2} + c_2\left(2\log 3 - \frac{3}{2}\right) \approx 2.6471$, with $q = 1 - e^{-1}$, $c_1 = \frac{2}{q} - \frac{q}{2 - q}$, $c_2 = \frac{3}{2q} - \frac{4 - q}{2(2 - q)}$; (d) $V - V_B = \frac{1}{2}(3 - c_1) + (\frac{3}{2} - c_2)(2\log 3 - \frac{3}{2}) > 0$; (e) since $nV_n^* \ge 0$, Fatou's lemma shows that $nV_n^*$ cannot converge in probability to $V$. So the ordinary bootstrap variance is inconsistent for an exactly unbiased, root-$n$ consistent estimated-propensity-score matching estimator.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] Treatment Propensity Function. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$. Then the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$.
